title: The Grammar
question: Plate I showed which objects reviewers inspect and which standards they argue from — are the two coupled, for each object, and has that coupling drifted over nine years?

figures.title: The grammar: which law judges which object
figures.deck: Five of twelve objects answer chiefly to their own law; the rest are judged under borrowed ones — design justification above all.

claims.statement: Five objects are judged first by their own named standard: novelty (67%), clarity (48%), robustness (33%), compute cost (32%), reproducibility (31%).
claims.derivation: row-normalized share of each object's units argued under its own namesake standard, for the 5 objects where that standard leads the row

claims.statement: Design justification is the most-used law for four other objects: empirical scope, method design, theory, and statistical rigor.
claims.derivation: count of objects whose row-normalized top standard is design_justification

claims.statement: Statistical rigor uses its nearest-named standard, identifiability, for just 9% of its units.

figures.title: The grammar's nine years: where P(standard | object) itself moved
figures.deck: The grammar is a habit, not a fashion: 138 of 144 cells stay inside the shuffle floor — and what little moved was mostly ground the novelty standard gave up.

claims.statement: 138 of the 144 (object, standard) cells stay inside the shuffle floor of ±4.05 percentage points between the 2018–19 and 2025–26 eras.
claims.derivation: count of the 12×12=144 (object, standard) cells where |delta[object][standard]| ≤ floor95 (0.0405)

claims.statement: Compute cost consolidated onto the cost-benefit standard, from 25.9% to 34.6% across nine years.
claims.derivation: P(standard='cost_benefit' | object='compute_cost') in the early (2018–19) vs. late (2025–26) era

claims.statement: Reproducibility consolidated onto its own norm, from 28.9% to 33.8% across nine years.
Problem framing's leading law, merit recognition, extended its lead from 22.5% to 30.2%, while the novelty standard (21.7%→15.4%) and presentation trust (11.4%→7.2%) receded on the same row.
Related work also slipped away from the novelty standard, from 34.7% to 28.6%.

caveats.text: Several standards are name-twins of their objects (novelty and the novelty standard, robustness and the robustness norm); for those cells a bright diagonal is partly analytic, since both labels can be responses to the same sentence.

Movers were re-checked within criticism and praise separately to rule out template effects, but a quieter drift in phrasing that the labeling model reads as a different rule cannot be excluded; every level rests on one model's reading, applied uniformly to both eras.
